git-and-nutrition/git-anatomy.sc: A labelled diagram shows the portal venous system with four marked sites of anastomosis between portal and systemic veins, including the lower esophagus and anal canal.
tk: Name the two systemic veins anastomosing with the left gastric vein at the lower esophagus.
State the clinical consequence of portal hypertension at this site.
Name the vessels anastomosing at the anal canal (portal vs systemic).
List one other site of porto-systemic anastomosis shown on the diagram.
ck: Identifies azygos/hemiazygos veins anastomosing with left gastric vein
States esophageal varices as the consequence at this site
Names superior rectal (portal) vs middle/inferior rectal (systemic) veins
Names a further correct site (e.g., paraumbilical veins with anterior abdominal wall veins, or retroperitoneal veins)

git-and-nutrition/git-anatomy.sc: A cross-sectional diagram of the upper abdomen shows the stomach, lesser omentum, greater omentum, and the lesser sac (omental bursa) behind the stomach.
tk: Name the structures forming the lesser omentum.
State the boundary that allows communication between the greater and lesser sacs.
Identify the structure lying immediately posterior to the stomach, in the floor of the lesser sac (stomach bed).
State the clinical relevance of the lesser sac in relation to pancreatic pathology.
ck: Names hepatogastric and hepatoduodenal ligaments as the lesser omentum
Identifies the epiploic (omental) foramen of Winslow
Names the pancreas as a major stomach bed structure
States pancreatic fluid/pseudocyst collections can accumulate in the lesser sac

git-and-nutrition/git-anatomy.t: Arterial Supply of the Gut - Watershed Areas
git-and-nutrition/git-anatomy.sc: A diagram of the abdominal aorta shows the celiac trunk, superior mesenteric artery, and inferior mesenteric artery, with two marked 'watershed' zones of relatively poor collateral supply.
tk: Name the gut regions supplied by each of the three named arteries based on embryological origin.
Identify the two clinically important watershed areas shown.
Explain why these watershed areas are vulnerable during hypotension.
Name the marginal artery that provides some collateral flow between the SMA and IMA territories.
ck: Correctly assigns foregut-celiac, midgut-SMA, hindgut-IMA
Identifies splenic flexure and rectosigmoid junction as watershed zones
Explains limited collateral anastomosis makes these areas prone to ischemic injury in low-flow states
Names the marginal artery of Drummond

git-and-nutrition/git-anatomy.sc: A diagram of the anterior abdominal wall shows the inguinal canal with its deep and superficial rings marked, along with the structures forming its walls.
tk: Name the boundaries (anterior, posterior, roof, floor) of the inguinal canal.
State the contents of the inguinal canal in a male.
Identify the anatomical landmark that differentiates a direct from an indirect inguinal hernia.
Name the structure that would be compressed at the deep ring in an indirect hernia.
ck: Correctly names external oblique aponeurosis (anterior), transversalis fascia/conjoint tendon (posterior), internal oblique/transversus arch (roof), inguinal ligament (floor)
States contents as spermatic cord (with its coverings) and ilioinguinal nerve
Identifies the inferior epigastric vessels as the landmark (medial = direct, lateral = indirect)
States the spermatic cord/processus vaginalis remnant passes through the deep ring in indirect hernia

git-and-nutrition/git-physiology.sc: A graph shows gastric acid output over time following a meal, with three labelled phases (cephalic, gastric, intestinal) of increasing then decreasing secretion.
tk: Name the three phases of gastric secretion shown and their principal triggers.
State the primary mediator responsible for the cephalic phase.
Explain the hormonal mechanism driving the gastric phase.
State the mechanism by which the intestinal phase inhibits further acid secretion.
ck: Names cephalic (sight/smell/taste), gastric (distension/peptides), intestinal (chyme in duodenum) phases
States vagal (parasympathetic) stimulation drives the cephalic phase
Explains gastrin release from G cells stimulating parietal cell acid secretion
States secretin and cholecystokinin/enterogastrone-mediated feedback inhibit acid secretion in the intestinal phase

git-and-nutrition/git-physiology.sc: A schematic of a gastric parietal cell shows the H+/K+-ATPase pump on the apical (canalicular) membrane, along with receptors for gastrin, histamine, and acetylcholine.
tk: Name the pump responsible for hydrogen ion secretion and its location.
Name the three receptors shown and their respective ligands.
Explain why histamine H2-receptor antagonists and proton pump inhibitors are both effective in reducing acid secretion.
State the enzyme within the parietal cell that supplies hydrogen ions for secretion.
ck: Identifies the H+/K+-ATPase (proton pump) on the apical/canalicular membrane
Names gastrin, histamine (H2), and acetylcholine (M3) receptors
Explains H2 blockers reduce histamine-driven stimulation while PPIs directly block the final common pump pathway
Names carbonic anhydrase as generating H+ from CO2 and water

git-and-nutrition/git-physiology.sc: A manometric tracing of small intestinal motility during the fasting state shows a cyclical pattern of quiescence, irregular contractions, and a burst of intense regular contractions, repeating approximately every 90-120 minutes.
tk: Name the motility pattern shown.
State the physiological purpose of this pattern.
Name the hormone most closely associated with initiating the intense contraction phase.
State what happens to this motility pattern after a meal is ingested.
ck: Identifies the migrating motor complex (MMC)
States its purpose as clearing residual food, secretions, and bacteria from the stomach and small intestine between meals ('housekeeper' function)
Names motilin as the key hormone
States the MMC is interrupted/abolished by feeding, replaced by fed-pattern motility

git-and-nutrition/git-physiology.sc: A diagram of an enterocyte's brush border and basolateral membrane shows labelled transporters for glucose, amino acids, and fatty acids.
tk: Name the apical transporter responsible for glucose and galactose absorption, and state its co-transported ion.
State the mechanism (facilitated vs active) by which fructose is absorbed.
Explain how absorbed long-chain fatty acids are packaged for transport into the lymphatics.
Name the basolateral transporter that moves glucose out of the enterocyte into the blood.
ck: Identifies SGLT1 (sodium-glucose cotransporter) for glucose/galactose
States fructose is absorbed by facilitated diffusion via GLUT5
Explains fatty acids are re-esterified to triglycerides and packaged into chylomicrons for lymphatic absorption
Names GLUT2 as the basolateral transporter

git-and-nutrition/liver-gallbladder-and-.sc: A diagram of a classic hepatic lobule shows a central vein, portal triads at the periphery, and hepatocytes divided into three concentric zones based on oxygen and nutrient gradient.
tk: Name the three zones of the hepatic lobule (Rappaport zonation).
State which zone is most susceptible to ischemic injury and why.
State which zone is most exposed to toxins absorbed from the gut and is most active in detoxification.
Name the components of a portal triad.
ck: Names Zone 1 (periportal), Zone 2 (intermediate), Zone 3 (centrilobular/pericentral)
Identifies Zone 3 as most vulnerable to hypoxia, being farthest from oxygenated blood supply
Identifies Zone 1 as first exposed to portal blood and most active in certain detoxification/metabolic functions
Names portal vein branch, hepatic artery branch, and bile duct

git-and-nutrition/liver-gallbladder-and-.sc: A flow chart shows the pathway of bilirubin from red cell breakdown through hepatic conjugation to excretion, with two forms of bilirubin (unconjugated and conjugated) marked at different stages.
tk: Name the enzyme responsible for conjugating bilirubin in hepatocytes.
Explain why unconjugated bilirubin is not water-soluble and cannot be excreted in urine.
State the fate of conjugated bilirubin after intestinal bacterial action.
Name the pigments responsible for the color of stool and urine, derived from this pathway.
ck: Names UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1)
Explains unconjugated bilirubin is lipid-soluble/protein-bound (albumin-bound), requiring conjugation for water solubility
States bacterial conversion to urobilinogen, then stercobilin (stool) and some reabsorbed urobilinogen excreted as urobilin (urine)
Names stercobilin (stool) and urobilin (urine)

git-and-nutrition/liver-gallbladder-and-.sc: A diagram shows the gallbladder, cystic duct, common bile duct, and duodenum, with a fatty meal indicated as the stimulus for a hormone released from the duodenal mucosa.
tk: Name the hormone released in response to fatty chyme in the duodenum.
State the two principal actions of this hormone relevant to bile delivery.
Name the sphincter that must relax to allow bile flow into the duodenum.
State one additional physiological action of this hormone beyond biliary/pancreatic effects.
ck: Names cholecystokinin (CCK)
States CCK causes gallbladder contraction and relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi
Names the sphincter of Oddi
States a valid additional action (e.g., stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion, promotes satiety)

git-and-nutrition/liver-gallbladder-and-.sc: A diagram of the exocrine pancreas shows acinar cells and duct cells, with two hormones labelled as stimulating different components of pancreatic juice.
tk: Name the hormone that primarily stimulates acinar cells to secrete digestive enzymes.
Name the hormone that primarily stimulates duct cells to secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid.
State the physiological purpose of the bicarbonate-rich secretion.
Name one proteolytic enzyme secreted in inactive (zymogen) form by acinar cells and its activator.
ck: Names cholecystokinin (CCK) for enzyme secretion
Names secretin for bicarbonate-rich fluid secretion
States bicarbonate neutralizes acidic chyme entering the duodenum, providing optimal pH for pancreatic enzymes
Names trypsinogen, activated by enterokinase (enteropeptidase) in the duodenal brush border

git-and-nutrition/git-histology-and-embr.sc: A photomicrograph shows finger-like projections lined by simple columnar epithelium with goblet cells, overlying a lamina propria containing a central lacteal.
tk: Identify the structure shown and the organ from which the slide is taken.
Name the function of the central lacteal visible within the villus.
Identify the specialized absorptive cell type covering the villus surface and its distinguishing microscopic feature.
Name the glands found at the base of the villi, between the crypts.
ck: Identifies an intestinal villus (small intestine)
States the lacteal absorbs and transports dietary lipids (as chylomicrons) into the lymphatic system
Identifies enterocytes with a brush border (microvilli)
Names the crypts of Lieberkühn (intestinal glands)

git-and-nutrition/git-histology-and-embr.sc: A photomicrograph shows an abrupt transition zone where stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium meets simple columnar epithelium.
tk: Identify the anatomical junction shown.
Name the epithelium type on each side of the junction.
State the clinical significance of this junction in relation to Barrett's esophagus.
Name the specific glands found within the submucosa of the esophagus, absent in the stomach wall.
ck: Identifies the gastroesophageal (squamocolumnar) junction
Correctly names stratified squamous non-keratinized (esophagus) and simple columnar (stomach)
States chronic acid reflux can cause metaplastic conversion of esophageal squamous epithelium to columnar (intestinal-type) epithelium, i.e., Barrett's esophagus
Names the esophageal submucosal glands

git-and-nutrition/git-histology-and-embr.sc: A sequence of three diagrams shows the midgut herniating into the umbilical cord, rotating, and returning to the abdominal cavity during embryonic development.
tk: State the total degree and direction of midgut rotation around the axis of the superior mesenteric artery.
Name the approximate gestational week at which physiological umbilical herniation occurs.
Identify the congenital anomaly that results from failure of the midgut to return to the abdominal cavity.
Name the anomaly resulting from incomplete rotation, predisposing to volvulus.
ck: States 270 degrees counterclockwise rotation
States physiological herniation occurs around week 6
Identifies omphalocele/exomphalos as the anomaly from failure of return
Names malrotation as predisposing to midgut volvulus

git-and-nutrition/git-histology-and-embr.sc: A diagram shows a small outpouching arising from the antimesenteric border of the ileum, labelled as a remnant of an embryonic structure.
tk: Name the embryological structure whose incomplete regression produces this anomaly.
State the 'rule of twos' commonly used to describe this anomaly's typical features.
Name the ectopic tissue types most commonly found within this diverticulum that can cause complications.
State the potential clinical complication of ectopic gastric mucosa within this structure.
ck: Names the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct
States the rule of twos (occurs in about 2% of population, within 2 feet of the ileocecal valve, about 2 inches long, often symptomatic before age 2, may contain 2 types of ectopic tissue)
Names ectopic gastric and/or pancreatic tissue
States ectopic gastric mucosa can secrete acid causing peptic ulceration and bleeding

git-and-nutrition/nutrition-and-metaboli.sc: A clinical photograph shows a patient with bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhages, and poor wound healing.
tk: Identify the vitamin deficiency most consistent with this presentation.
State the biochemical role of this vitamin relevant to the findings shown.
Name one dietary source rich in this vitamin.
State the name of the clinical syndrome caused by this deficiency.
ck: Identifies vitamin C (ascorbic acid) deficiency
States its role as a cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase in collagen synthesis
Names a valid source (e.g., citrus fruits, guava, amla)
Names scurvy

git-and-nutrition/nutrition-and-metaboli.sc: A schematic shows a fatty acid chain undergoing repeated cycles of a four-step enzymatic pathway within the mitochondrial matrix, producing acetyl-CoA units.
tk: Name the pathway shown and its cellular location.
Name the transport molecule required to move long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondrial matrix.
State the products of one cycle of this pathway.
Explain how the acetyl-CoA produced is subsequently used for energy production.
ck: Names beta-oxidation, occurring in the mitochondrial matrix
Names carnitine (carnitine shuttle/CPT I and II system)
States each cycle produces one acetyl-CoA, one FADH2, and one NADH, shortening the fatty acid chain by two carbons
States acetyl-CoA enters the citric acid (Krebs) cycle for further oxidation and ATP generation

git-and-nutrition/nutrition-and-metaboli.sc: Two clinical photographs are shown side by side: one of a severely wasted child with visible ribs and no edema, and another of a child with generalized edema, a distended abdomen, and flaky skin lesions despite adequate calorie intake but severe protein deficiency.
tk: Identify the condition shown in each photograph.
Explain the biochemical basis for the edema seen in the second condition.
State the typical calorie versus protein intake pattern distinguishing the two conditions.
Name one skin or hair finding characteristic of the edematous condition.
ck: Identifies marasmus (first) and kwashiorkor (second)
Explains kwashiorkor's edema results from hypoalbuminemia reducing plasma oncotic pressure
States marasmus involves severe deficiency of both calories and protein, while kwashiorkor involves relatively preserved calories with severe protein deficiency
Names a valid finding (e.g., flaky-paint dermatosis, hair depigmentation/'flag sign')

git-and-nutrition/nutrition-and-metaboli.sc: A diagram shows lactate produced by anaerobic glycolysis in skeletal muscle being transported to the liver, converted back to glucose, and returned to the muscle via the bloodstream.
tk: Name the cycle depicted.
State the metabolic condition in muscle that leads to lactate production.
Name the hepatic process by which lactate is converted back into glucose.
Explain the overall energetic cost of this cycle to the body (which organ expends net ATP).
ck: Names the Cori cycle
States anaerobic conditions (e.g., strenuous exercise) causing pyruvate to be reduced to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase
Names hepatic gluconeogenesis
States the liver expends net ATP to regenerate glucose, shifting the energetic burden from muscle to liver

renal/renal-anatomy.sc: A bisected kidney specimen is displayed showing the outer cortex, inner medulla with renal pyramids, and a central renal sinus containing the pelvis and calyces.
tk: Identify the cortex, medulla, and renal pyramids on the specimen.
Name the structure formed by the union of major calyces.
State the name given to the medullary tissue extending into the cortex between pyramids.
Name the structure that carries urine from the renal pelvis to the bladder.
ck: Correctly identifies cortex (outer, granular) and medulla (inner, striated pyramids)
Names the renal pelvis
Names the renal columns (of Bertin)
Names the ureter

renal/renal-anatomy.sc: A diagram shows the renal artery dividing into segmental, interlobar, arcuate, and interlobular arteries before terminating in afferent arterioles.
tk: List the order of arterial branching from the renal artery to the afferent arteriole.
State the location of arcuate arteries relative to the corticomedullary junction.
Name the vessel that carries blood away from the glomerulus.
Explain why the kidney is relatively resistant to venous infarction compared to some other organs.
ck: Lists segmental, interlobar, arcuate, interlobular (cortical radiate) arteries, then afferent arterioles
States arcuate arteries run along the corticomedullary junction
Names the efferent arteriole
Explains extensive collateral/anastomotic venous drainage or dual capillary bed (glomerular and peritubular) reduces infarction risk relative to purely end-arterial organs

renal/renal-anatomy.t: Renal Fascia and Perirenal Space Diagram
renal/renal-anatomy.sc: A transverse cross-sectional diagram of the posterior abdominal wall shows the kidney surrounded by perirenal fat, enclosed within a fascial layer, with pararenal fat external to this layer.
tk: Name the fascial layer enclosing the kidney and perirenal fat.
State the clinical relevance of this fascial arrangement in relation to spread of perinephric abscess or blood.
Identify the vertebral level at which the kidneys are typically located.
State why the right kidney is usually slightly lower than the left.
ck: Names the renal (Gerota's) fascia
States the fascia can contain and localize collections such as blood or pus within the perirenal space, at least initially
States approximately T12 to L3 vertebral level
States displacement by the liver on the right side

renal/renal-anatomy.sc: A diagram of the course of the ureter from the renal pelvis to the bladder shows three marked sites of physiological narrowing.
tk: Name the three sites of ureteric constriction.
State the clinical significance of these constrictions in relation to renal calculi.
Name the vessel that crosses anterior to the ureter near the pelvic brim.
State the structure crossed by the ureter close to the cervix/vas deferens in the pelvis.
ck: Names pelviureteric junction, crossing of the pelvic brim (iliac vessels), and vesicoureteric junction
States these are common sites for ureteric stones to become lodged
Names the gonadal (ovarian/testicular) vessels crossing anteriorly near the pelvic brim, or the common/external iliac vessels
States the uterine artery crosses anterior to the ureter in females ('water under the bridge'), or the vas deferens crosses anterior in males

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.sc: An electron micrograph-style diagram shows the three layers of the glomerular filtration barrier: fenestrated endothelium, basement membrane, and podocyte foot processes with filtration slits.
tk: Name the three layers of the filtration barrier shown.
State which layer is primarily responsible for size-selective filtration of larger proteins.
Explain the basis of charge-selective filtration at this barrier.
Name the condition resulting from loss of the negatively charged barrier, causing selective albuminuria.
ck: Names fenestrated endothelium, glomerular basement membrane, podocyte foot processes/filtration slits
States the basement membrane and slit diaphragm provide the main size restriction for large proteins
Explains negatively charged heparan sulfate proteoglycans repel negatively charged plasma proteins like albumin
Names minimal change disease (or nephrotic syndrome with loss of charge barrier)

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.sc: Laboratory values are provided: urine inulin concentration, plasma inulin concentration, and urine flow rate, along with the formula for clearance.
tk: Calculate the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) using the inulin clearance formula from the given values.
Explain why inulin is considered an ideal marker for measuring GFR.
State one substance commonly used clinically as an estimate of GFR, and why it is less accurate than inulin.
State the approximate normal GFR value in a healthy young adult.
ck: Correctly applies clearance = (urine concentration x urine flow rate) / plasma concentration
States inulin is freely filtered, not reabsorbed, not secreted, and not metabolized by the kidney
Names creatinine, noting it is slightly secreted by the tubules, causing mild overestimation of true GFR
States approximately 120-125 mL/min

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.sc: A diagram of the loop of Henle shows the descending and ascending limbs with different permeabilities to water and solutes, generating an increasing osmotic gradient toward the medulla.
tk: State the water and solute permeability of the descending versus ascending limb.
Explain how active transport in the thick ascending limb contributes to generating the medullary gradient.
Name the transporter responsible for active NaCl reabsorption in the thick ascending limb.
State the physiological purpose of the medullary concentration gradient established by this mechanism.
ck: States descending limb is water-permeable but relatively impermeable to solutes, while thick ascending limb is water-impermeable but actively transports solutes
Explains active NaCl reabsorption in the ascending limb without water contributes to the hyperosmotic medullary interstitium
Names the Na+/K+/2Cl- (NKCC2) cotransporter
States the gradient enables the kidney to produce concentrated urine via the collecting duct under ADH influence

renal/renal-physiology-filtration-reabso.sc: A graph shows filtered glucose load, reabsorbed glucose, and excreted glucose plotted against increasing plasma glucose concentration, with excretion beginning to rise sharply beyond a certain plasma concentration.
tk: Name the phenomenon at which glucose begins to appear in the urine.
State the approximate plasma glucose concentration at which this occurs (renal threshold).
Name the transporter primarily responsible for glucose reabsorption in the early proximal tubule.
Explain why glucose reabsorption capacity is described as having a transport maximum (Tm).
ck: Names the renal threshold for glucose
States approximately 180-200 mg/dL
Names SGLT2 (in the early proximal convoluted tubule)
Explains a finite number of transporters become saturated, so once all are occupied, additional filtered glucose cannot be reabsorbed and is excreted

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.sc: An arterial blood gas report shows pH 7.30, PaCO2 55 mmHg, and HCO3- 26 mEq/L.
tk: Identify the primary acid-base disturbance shown.
State whether metabolic or renal compensation is evident from the given values.
Name one clinical condition that could produce this pattern.
State the renal mechanism that would compensate for this disturbance if it became chronic.
ck: Identifies respiratory acidosis (low pH, elevated PaCO2)
States minimal renal compensation is evident yet (HCO3- only mildly elevated), consistent with an acute or early process
Names a valid cause (e.g., COPD exacerbation, opioid overdose, neuromuscular respiratory failure)
States the kidney would increase H+ secretion and HCO3- reabsorption/generation over 3-5 days to compensate

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.sc: A diagram of an intercalated cell in the collecting duct shows a proton pump on the apical membrane and a bicarbonate-chloride exchanger on the basolateral membrane.
tk: Name the type of intercalated cell shown (type A or type B) and state which handles acidosis.
Name the apical transporter responsible for hydrogen ion secretion.
Explain the fate of bicarbonate generated within the cell during this process.
Name the two urinary buffer systems that allow continued H+ secretion without dramatically lowering urine pH.
ck: Identifies type A intercalated cells as responding to acidosis with H+ secretion
Names the H+-ATPase (and/or H+/K+-ATPase) pump
States generated bicarbonate is reabsorbed into blood via the basolateral Cl-/HCO3- exchanger
Names phosphate (titratable acid) buffer and ammonia/ammonium buffer systems

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.sc: Laboratory values are provided: serum sodium, chloride, and bicarbonate, with a clinical history of diabetic ketoacidosis.
tk: Calculate the anion gap using the given values and standard formula.
State the expected anion gap finding in diabetic ketoacidosis and explain why.
Name one other cause of a high anion gap metabolic acidosis.
Name one cause of a normal (non-elevated) anion gap metabolic acidosis for comparison.
ck: Correctly applies anion gap = Na+ - (Cl- + HCO3-)
States an elevated anion gap due to accumulation of unmeasured ketoacid anions (beta-hydroxybutyrate, acetoacetate)
Names a valid cause (e.g., lactic acidosis, uremia, methanol/ethylene glycol toxicity, salicylate poisoning)
Names a valid cause (e.g., diarrhea, renal tubular acidosis)

renal/acid-base-balance-and-renal-regula.sc: A diagram of a proximal tubule cell shows glutamine metabolism generating ammonium ion and bicarbonate, with the ammonium ion secreted into the tubular lumen.
tk: Name the amino acid substrate metabolized to generate ammonium and bicarbonate.
State the fate of the bicarbonate generated by this reaction.
Explain how increased renal ammoniagenesis assists in chronic metabolic acidosis.
State the transporter/mechanism by which ammonium is secreted into the tubular fluid.
ck: Names glutamine
States the generated bicarbonate (new bicarbonate) is reabsorbed into the blood, helping correct acidosis
Explains chronic acidosis upregulates renal glutamine metabolism/ammoniagenesis, increasing capacity for net acid excretion
States ammonium is secreted via substitution for H+ on the Na+/H+ exchanger (or as NH3 diffusion trapped as NH4+ in acidic lumen)

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.sc: A photomicrograph shows a renal corpuscle with a tuft of capillaries surrounded by a two-layered epithelial capsule, with a visible urinary (Bowman's) space between the layers.
tk: Name the structure shown and its two epithelial layers.
Identify the specialized cells forming the visceral layer.
Name the space between the parietal and visceral layers and state its function.
Identify the pole of the corpuscle where the proximal convoluted tubule begins.
ck: Identifies the renal corpuscle with parietal and visceral layers of Bowman's capsule
Names podocytes as forming the visceral layer
Names Bowman's (urinary) space, which collects the glomerular filtrate
Names the urinary pole

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.t: Proximal vs Distal Convoluted Tubule Slide
renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.sc: A photomicrograph shows two adjacent tubule cross-sections: one lined by large cells with a prominent brush border and eosinophilic cytoplasm, and another lined by smaller cells with no brush border and a wider visible lumen.
tk: Identify which tubule segment is which, based on the described features.
State the histological basis for the brush border seen in one tubule type.
Explain why proximal tubule cells appear more eosinophilic than distal tubule cells.
Name a functional difference between the two segments relevant to sodium reabsorption.
ck: Identifies the brush-bordered cells as proximal convoluted tubule and the other as distal convoluted tubule
States the brush border consists of long, densely packed microvilli increasing absorptive surface area
Explains abundant mitochondria supporting active transport give proximal tubule cells more eosinophilic cytoplasm
States the proximal tubule reabsorbs the bulk (~65%) of filtered sodium isosmotically, while the distal tubule performs fine, hormonally regulated adjustment

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.sc: A sequential diagram shows the ureteric bud arising from the mesonephric duct and inducing the metanephric mesenchyme to form nephrons.
tk: Name the embryonic structure that gives rise to the collecting duct system and ureter.
Name the embryonic tissue that gives rise to the nephron (glomerulus to distal tubule).
State the reciprocal inductive relationship between these two structures.
Name the congenital anomaly resulting from failure of the ureteric bud to reach the metanephric mesenchyme.
ck: Names the ureteric bud (metanephric diverticulum)
Names the metanephric mesenchyme (metanephric blastema)
Explains the ureteric bud induces mesenchyme to differentiate into nephrons, while the mesenchyme induces branching of the ureteric bud
Names renal agenesis

renal/renal-histology-and-embryology.sc: A diagram shows the normal ascent of the kidney from the pelvis to the lumbar region during development, alongside an abnormal image showing fused lower poles of both kidneys connected across the midline.
tk: Name the normal process depicted by the ascent of the kidney.
Identify the anomaly shown in the second image.
State the structure that typically prevents this fused kidney from ascending to its normal position.
Name one clinical complication associated with this anomaly.
ck: Names ascent (and relative rotation) of the kidney from the pelvis to the lumbar (retroperitoneal) region
Identifies horseshoe kidney
States the inferior mesenteric artery typically obstructs further ascent, trapping the fused kidney inferiorly
Names a valid complication (e.g., increased risk of infection, obstruction, or stone formation due to abnormal drainage)

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.sc: A diagram of the principal cell of the collecting duct shows ADH binding a receptor on the basolateral membrane, triggering insertion of water channels into the apical membrane.
tk: Name the receptor and water channel involved in ADH action.
State the second messenger pathway activated by ADH binding.
Explain the physiological trigger for increased ADH secretion.
State what would happen to urine concentration in the absence of ADH (e.g., central diabetes insipidus).
ck: Names the V2 receptor and aquaporin-2 water channels
States cAMP-mediated pathway (via Gs protein and adenylyl cyclase) triggering AQP2 insertion
States increased plasma osmolality (sensed by hypothalamic osmoreceptors) or decreased blood volume/pressure stimulates ADH release
States production of large volumes of dilute urine, due to inability to reabsorb water in the collecting duct

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.sc: A flow chart shows renin, angiotensinogen, angiotensin I, ACE, angiotensin II, and aldosterone, with feedback arrows to blood pressure and blood volume.
tk: Trace the pathway from renin release to aldosterone secretion.
Name the organ where angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) is most active.
State two physiological actions of angiotensin II besides stimulating aldosterone release.
Explain how aldosterone raises blood pressure/volume at the level of the nephron.
ck: Correctly traces renin cleaving angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, ACE converting it to angiotensin II, which stimulates aldosterone release from the adrenal zona glomerulosa
Names the lungs (pulmonary vascular endothelium) as the primary site of ACE activity
States valid actions (e.g., vasoconstriction, stimulation of thirst, ADH release)
Explains aldosterone increases sodium (and water) reabsorption and potassium secretion in the distal nephron/collecting duct, expanding extracellular volume

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.t: Potassium Balance and ECG Correlation Station
renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.sc: An ECG strip is shown displaying peaked T waves and a widened QRS complex, alongside a laboratory report showing an elevated serum potassium level.
tk: Identify the electrolyte disturbance most consistent with the ECG findings.
Explain the physiological basis for peaked T waves in this condition.
Name one hormone that promotes cellular potassium uptake, useful in emergency management.
State one renal mechanism by which the kidney normally excretes excess potassium.
ck: Identifies hyperkalemia
Explains altered resting membrane potential and faster repolarization due to elevated extracellular potassium affecting cardiac myocyte excitability
Names insulin (with glucose) as promoting intracellular potassium shift
States aldosterone-stimulated potassium secretion in the principal cells of the collecting duct

renal/fluid-electrolyte-and-renal-endocr.sc: A diagram shows peritubular interstitial cells in the renal cortex producing a hormone in response to tissue hypoxia, stimulating red blood cell production in the bone marrow.
tk: Name the hormone produced by the kidney in this diagram.
State the stimulus for increased secretion of this hormone.
Explain why patients with chronic kidney disease commonly develop anemia.
Name the therapeutic agent used clinically to treat this type of anemia.
ck: Names erythropoietin
States tissue/renal hypoxia as the stimulus
Explains damaged renal peritubular cells produce insufficient erythropoietin, reducing bone marrow stimulation for red cell production
Names recombinant human erythropoietin (or erythropoiesis-stimulating agents)

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.sc: A diagram of the base of the brain shows the arterial circle formed by the anterior and posterior circulations, with connecting communicating arteries labelled.
tk: Name the vessels that form the anterior and posterior communicating arteries' connections.
State the physiological purpose of this arterial circle.
Identify the artery most commonly affected in a stroke causing contralateral leg weakness greater than arm weakness.
Name the artery whose occlusion classically produces contralateral face and arm weakness with expressive aphasia if the dominant hemisphere is affected.
ck: Correctly identifies the circle formed by internal carotid, anterior cerebral, posterior cerebral, and communicating arteries
States it provides collateral circulation, protecting against ischemia if one contributing vessel is occluded
Names the anterior cerebral artery
Names the middle cerebral artery

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.sc: A horizontal section diagram of the cerebrum shows the internal capsule divided into anterior limb, genu, and posterior limb, with labelled fiber tracts passing through each part.
tk: Name the fiber tract passing through the genu of the internal capsule.
Name the fiber tract passing through the posterior limb, responsible for voluntary limb movement.
Explain why a small lacunar infarct in the internal capsule can cause a dense contralateral hemiparesis.
Name the blood vessels most commonly responsible for lacunar infarcts in this region.
ck: Names corticobulbar fibers at the genu
Names corticospinal (pyramidal) tract fibers in the posterior limb
Explains the internal capsule densely concentrates descending motor fibers in a small area, so even a small lesion affects a large proportion of fibers
Names the lenticulostriate arteries (branches of the middle cerebral artery)

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.sc: A cross-sectional diagram of the pons is shown with several labelled nuclei, including one associated with lateral gaze and one associated with facial expression.
tk: Name the cranial nerve nuclei labelled in the pons relevant to lateral gaze and facial expression.
State the effect of a lesion at the abducens nucleus on eye movement.
Explain the anatomical basis of 'one-and-a-half syndrome' involving the abducens nucleus and medial longitudinal fasciculus.
Name the cranial nerve that exits at the cerebellopontine angle alongside the facial nerve.
ck: Names the abducens (CN VI) nucleus and facial (CN VII) nucleus
States loss of ipsilateral lateral rectus function, causing inability to abduct that eye
Explains combined lesion of the abducens nucleus/PPRF and the MLF produces ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy plus internuclear ophthalmoplegia
Names the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII)

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.sc: A schematic diagram shows the direct and indirect pathways of the basal ganglia circuit connecting the striatum, globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, and thalamus.
tk: Name the structures forming the striatum.
State the net effect of the direct pathway on movement.
State the net effect of the indirect pathway on movement.
Explain how loss of dopaminergic input in Parkinson's disease shifts the balance between these pathways.
ck: Names caudate nucleus and putamen as the striatum
States the direct pathway facilitates/increases movement (disinhibits the thalamus)
States the indirect pathway inhibits/suppresses movement (increases thalamic inhibition)
Explains dopamine loss reduces direct pathway facilitation and increases indirect pathway inhibition, favoring bradykinesia and rigidity

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.sc: A cross-sectional diagram of the spinal cord at the cervical level shows the dorsal columns, lateral corticospinal tract, and lateral spinothalamic tract labelled in the white matter.
tk: Name the modality carried by the dorsal columns.
Name the modality carried by the lateral spinothalamic tract.
State the level at which each of these two sensory pathways decussates.
Explain the resulting pattern of sensory loss in a hemisection (Brown-Sequard) lesion of the cord.
ck: States dorsal columns carry fine touch, vibration, and proprioception
States the spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature
States dorsal columns decussate in the medulla (as internal arcuate fibers), while spinothalamic fibers decussate near their level of entry in the spinal cord
Explains ipsilateral loss of fine touch/proprioception and motor function with contralateral loss of pain/temperature below the lesion

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.sc: A labelled diagram of the brachial plexus shows roots, trunks, divisions, cords, and terminal branches, with one nerve highlighted arising from the posterior cord.
tk: Name the five terminal branches of the brachial plexus.
Identify the nerve highlighted from the posterior cord and its major motor function.
Name the injury pattern (roots involved) responsible for Erb's palsy and describe the resulting arm position.
Name the injury pattern responsible for Klumpke's palsy.
ck: Names musculocutaneous, axillary, radial, median, and ulnar nerves
Identifies the radial nerve, responsible for extension of the elbow, wrist, and fingers
States C5-C6 root injury producing the 'waiter's tip' position (arm adducted, internally rotated, extended, pronated)
States C8-T1 root injury, often with a claw hand deformity

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.sc: A body dermatome map is displayed with a specific dermatome band highlighted at the level of the nipple line.
tk: Identify the spinal cord segment corresponding to the highlighted dermatome.
Explain the clinical utility of dermatome mapping in localizing spinal cord or nerve root lesions.
Name the dermatome level corresponding to the umbilicus.
State the sensory testing method typically used to map dermatomes at the bedside.
ck: Identifies T4 as corresponding to the nipple line
Explains a defined sensory loss pattern along a dermatome can help localize the level of a spinal cord or root lesion
States T10 corresponds to the umbilicus
States light touch and pinprick testing are used to assess dermatomal sensation

nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.t: Lumbosacral Plexus and Sciatic Nerve Diagram
nervous-system-neurosciences/neuroanatom.sc: A diagram of the lumbosacral plexus shows the sciatic nerve formed from L4-S3 roots, dividing into tibial and common peroneal (fibular) components near the popliteal fossa.
tk: Name the two terminal branches of the sciatic nerve.
State the muscle groups supplied by the common peroneal (fibular) nerve and its typical injury presentation.
State the muscle groups supplied by the tibial nerve.
Name the site most vulnerable to common peroneal nerve injury and why.
ck: Names the tibial nerve and common peroneal (fibular) nerve
States the common peroneal nerve supplies ankle dorsiflexors/evertors, injury causing foot drop
States the tibial nerve supplies the posterior leg muscles (plantarflexors/invertors)
Names the neck of the fibula, where the nerve is superficial and vulnerable to compression or trauma

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.sc: A graph of membrane potential against time during a neuronal action potential is shown, with labelled phases including resting potential, depolarization, overshoot, repolarization, and after-hyperpolarization.
tk: Name the ion channel primarily responsible for the rapid depolarization phase.
Name the ion channel primarily responsible for repolarization.
Explain the ionic basis of the after-hyperpolarization phase.
State the approximate resting membrane potential of a typical neuron.
ck: Names voltage-gated sodium channels for depolarization
Names voltage-gated (delayed rectifier) potassium channels for repolarization
Explains continued potassium efflux after the action potential (channels slow to close) drives the membrane potential transiently more negative than resting potential
States approximately -70 mV

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.sc: A diagram of a chemical synapse shows a presynaptic terminal with synaptic vesicles, a synaptic cleft, and postsynaptic receptors.
tk: Describe the sequence of events from action potential arrival to neurotransmitter release.
Name the ion whose influx into the presynaptic terminal triggers vesicle fusion.
Explain the difference between an EPSP and an IPSP in terms of the postsynaptic ion channels involved.
State the process by which neurotransmitter action is terminated at a cholinergic synapse.
ck: Describes depolarization opening voltage-gated calcium channels, calcium influx triggering vesicle docking/fusion, and neurotransmitter release by exocytosis
Names calcium (Ca2+)
States EPSPs typically involve opening of sodium/cation channels causing depolarization, while IPSPs typically involve chloride or potassium channels causing hyperpolarization
States acetylcholinesterase enzymatically degrades acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.sc: A diagram of the knee-jerk (patellar) reflex is shown with the muscle spindle, afferent Ia fiber, spinal cord synapse, and efferent motor neuron labelled.
tk: Name the type of reflex demonstrated and its afferent fiber type.
State the number of synapses involved in this reflex arc.
Explain the physiological role of the muscle spindle in this reflex.
Name the reciprocal inhibition mechanism that relaxes the antagonist muscle during this reflex.
ck: Identifies a monosynaptic myotatic (stretch) reflex with Ia afferent fibers
States it is monosynaptic (single synapse between afferent and efferent neuron)
Explains the muscle spindle detects stretch of the muscle, triggering a reflex contraction to resist the stretch
Names Ia inhibitory interneuron-mediated reciprocal inhibition of the antagonist muscle

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurophysio.sc: A diagram traces CSF production in the choroid plexus, flow through the ventricular system, and absorption via arachnoid granulations into the venous sinuses.
tk: Name the structure responsible for CSF production.
Trace the pathway of CSF flow from the lateral ventricles to its site of absorption.
Name the narrow channel connecting the third and fourth ventricles, a common site of obstruction.
State the consequence of obstruction at this narrow channel.
ck: Names the choroid plexus

Traces lateral ventricles to third ventricle via interventricular foramina (of Monro), to fourth ventricle via cerebral aqueduct, then to subarachnoid space via foramina of Luschka/Magendie, and absorption via arachnoid granulations into dural venous sinuses
Names the cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius)
States obstructive (non-communicating) hydrocephalus with dilation of the lateral and third ventricles

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.sc: A photomicrograph of a large multipolar neuron shows a prominent nucleus with a visible nucleolus, and basophilic granular material in the cytoplasm.
tk: Identify the basophilic granular structures seen in the cytoplasm.
State the functional significance of these structures.
Explain why these structures are typically absent from the axon hillock and axon.
Name the process by which these structures increase in size and activity following axonal injury.
ck: Identifies Nissl bodies (rough endoplasmic reticulum with ribosomes)
States they are the site of protein synthesis, supporting neuronal maintenance and repair
Explains protein synthesis machinery is concentrated in the soma/dendrites, while the axon and axon hillock lack ribosomes
Names chromatolysis (central chromatolysis) as the reactive change following axonal injury

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.sc: An electron micrograph shows a single large-diameter axon surrounded by concentric myelin lamellae, produced by a single supporting cell.
tk: Name the myelinating cell shown and state the ratio of myelinating cells to axons in the peripheral nervous system for large myelinated fibers.
Contrast this with the myelinating pattern in the central nervous system.
Name the gap between adjacent myelin segments and its functional significance.
State one demyelinating disease affecting the peripheral nervous system.
ck: Names the Schwann cell, noting one Schwann cell myelinates one internode of one axon (1:1 for large myelinated fibers)
Contrasts with oligodendrocytes, each of which myelinates multiple axons/internodes in the CNS
Names the node of Ranvier, essential for saltatory conduction
Names a valid condition (e.g., Guillain-Barre syndrome, Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease)

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.sc: A sequential diagram shows the neural plate folding to form the neural tube, with neural crest cells shown migrating away from the tube's dorsal margins.
tk: Name the process by which the neural plate becomes the neural tube.
Name two derivatives of neural crest cells.
State the region of the neural tube that gives rise to the brain versus the spinal cord.
Name the vitamin whose deficiency is most strongly linked to neural tube defects.
ck: Names neurulation
Names valid derivatives (e.g., dorsal root ganglia, autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, melanocytes, adrenal medulla)
States the cephalic (cranial) end forms brain vesicles, while the caudal portion forms the spinal cord
Names folic acid

nervous-system-neurosciences/neurohistol.sc: A diagram shows astrocytic end-feet surrounding a brain capillary, with tight junctions labelled between adjacent endothelial cells.
tk: Name the glial cell type shown and its contribution to the blood-brain barrier.
State the structural feature of the endothelial cells that limits paracellular movement of substances.
Explain why lipid-soluble substances cross the blood-brain barrier more readily than water-soluble ones.
Name one clinical circumstance in which the blood-brain barrier is disrupted, altering drug or substance penetration.
ck: Names astrocytes, whose end-feet help induce and maintain endothelial tight junctions
Identifies tight junctions between endothelial cells as limiting paracellular diffusion
Explains lipid-soluble molecules can diffuse directly through the endothelial cell membrane, while water-soluble substances require specific transporters
Names a valid example (e.g., bacterial meningitis, brain tumor, stroke, trauma)

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.sc: A diagram shows two autonomic pathways from the central nervous system to a target organ, one with a short preganglionic and long postganglionic fiber, and the other with the reverse pattern.
tk: Identify which pathway represents sympathetic and which represents parasympathetic outflow.
Name the neurotransmitter released at all autonomic ganglia (preganglionic to postganglionic synapse).
Name the neurotransmitter typically released by postganglionic sympathetic fibers to most target organs.
State one organ where the postganglionic sympathetic neurotransmitter is atypically acetylcholine rather than the usual transmitter.
ck: Identifies short preganglionic/long postganglionic as sympathetic and long preganglionic/short postganglionic as parasympathetic
Names acetylcholine (nicotinic receptors) at all autonomic ganglia
Names norepinephrine as the typical postganglionic sympathetic transmitter
Names sweat glands (or in some accounts, some blood vessels supplying skeletal muscle) as the exception

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.sc: A diagram of the hypothalamus shows several labelled nuclei, including one associated with satiety, one with hunger, and one with circadian rhythm.
tk: Name the nucleus associated with satiety and state the effect of its bilateral destruction.
Name the nucleus associated with hunger/feeding drive.
Name the nucleus responsible for circadian rhythm generation and its main afferent input.
Name the hypothalamic nucleus most directly responsible for thermoregulatory heat-loss responses.
ck: Names the ventromedial nucleus, noting its destruction leads to hyperphagia and obesity
Names the lateral hypothalamic nucleus (feeding/hunger center)
Names the suprachiasmatic nucleus, receiving direct retinal input for light entrainment
Names the anterior hypothalamus (heat-loss center, e.g., promoting sweating and vasodilation)

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.sc: A diagram of the limbic system shows the hippocampus, amygdala, fornix, and mammillary bodies interconnected in the Papez circuit.
tk: Name the structure primarily responsible for consolidation of new long-term declarative memory.
Name the structure primarily responsible for the emotional significance (especially fear) of a stimulus.
Explain the clinical consequence of bilateral hippocampal damage on memory function.
Name the pathway connecting the hippocampus to the mammillary bodies.
ck: Names the hippocampus
Names the amygdala
States anterograde amnesia (inability to form new long-term declarative memories) with relatively preserved older memories and procedural learning
Names the fornix

nervous-system-neurosciences/autonomic-n.sc: Two EEG tracings are shown: one with low-amplitude, high-frequency desynchronized activity resembling wakefulness alongside evidence of rapid eye movements, and another with high-amplitude slow delta waves.
tk: Identify the sleep stage represented by each tracing.
State the physiological changes in muscle tone characteristic of the REM stage.
Name the sleep stage in which sleepwalking and night terrors typically occur.
State the approximate proportion of total sleep time typically spent in REM sleep in a healthy young adult.
ck: Identifies REM sleep (desynchronized EEG with rapid eye movements) and slow-wave (stage N3) sleep (delta waves)
States near-complete skeletal muscle atonia during REM sleep (except extraocular and respiratory muscles)
States slow-wave (deep, non-REM stage N3) sleep
States approximately 20-25%

special-senses/eye-anatomy-and-visual-pa.sc: A diagram shows the six extraocular muscles and their primary lines of pull on the globe, with the eye in the primary anatomical position.
tk: Name the extraocular muscle primarily responsible for depression of the eye when it is abducted.
Name the muscle primarily responsible for depression when the eye is adducted.
Name the cranial nerves supplying the superior oblique and lateral rectus muscles.
State the classic head tilt test used to assess superior oblique palsy.
ck: Names the inferior rectus (depresses the abducted eye)
Names the superior oblique (depresses the adducted eye)
Names the trochlear nerve (CN IV) for superior oblique and abducens nerve (CN VI) for lateral rectus
Names the Bielschowsky head tilt test

special-senses/eye-anatomy-and-visual-pa.sc: A set of four visual field diagrams is shown, each depicting a different pattern of visual field loss, with a corresponding lesion site to be identified for one selected diagram showing bitemporal hemianopia.
tk: Identify the visual field defect shown.
Name the anatomical structure whose lesion produces this pattern.
Explain, in terms of nerve fiber decussation, why this specific pattern results.
Name one common cause of a lesion at this site.
ck: Identifies bitemporal hemianopia
Localizes the lesion to the optic chiasm
Explains only the nasal retinal fibers (representing the temporal visual fields) decussate at the chiasm, so a central chiasmal lesion affects fibers from both nasal retinas
Names a valid cause (e.g., pituitary adenoma compressing the chiasm from below)

special-senses/eye-anatomy-and-visual-pa.t: Anterior Chamber Angle and Aqueous Outflow Diagram
special-senses/eye-anatomy-and-visual-pa.sc: A diagram of the anterior segment of the eye shows aqueous humor produced by the ciliary body, circulating through the posterior and anterior chambers, and draining at the iridocorneal angle.
tk: Name the structure responsible for aqueous humor production.
Name the main structure through which aqueous humor drains from the anterior chamber.
Explain the consequence of outflow obstruction at this angle on intraocular pressure.
Name the clinical condition resulting from acute angle closure and the presenting symptom of eye pain with halos around lights.
ck: Names the ciliary body (ciliary processes/non-pigmented epithelium)
Names the trabecular meshwork draining into the canal of Schlemm
Explains obstruction to outflow raises intraocular pressure due to continued aqueous production without adequate drainage
Names acute angle-closure glaucoma

special-senses/eye-anatomy-and-visual-pa.sc: A fundus photograph shows the optic disc with a normal cup-to-disc ratio, along with the central retinal artery and vein emerging from its center.
tk: Name the structure corresponding to the optic disc anatomically (what it represents).
Explain why the optic disc corresponds to a natural blind spot in the visual field.
Name the vessels visible at the optic disc and their embryological/anatomical origin.
State the expected fundoscopic finding in raised intracranial pressure at this site.
ck: Identifies the optic disc as the point where retinal ganglion cell axons converge to exit as the optic nerve
Explains there are no photoreceptors at this location, since it is occupied by nerve fibers rather than retina
Names the central retinal artery and vein, branches/tributaries of the ophthalmic vessels
States papilledema (disc swelling with blurred margins)

special-senses/ear-anatomy-and-vestibula.sc: A diagram of the middle ear shows the three ossicles connecting the tympanic membrane to the oval window, with two small muscles labelled attaching to two of the ossicles.
tk: Name the three ossicles in order from the tympanic membrane to the oval window.
Name the two muscles of the middle ear and the ossicle each attaches to.
State the functional role of the ossicular chain in impedance matching.
Name the nerves supplying each of the two middle ear muscles.
ck: Names malleus, incus, stapes in order
Names tensor tympani (attaching to malleus) and stapedius (attaching to stapes)
Explains the ossicular lever mechanism and the area ratio between tympanic membrane and oval window amplify sound pressure, compensating for the air-to-fluid impedance mismatch
Names the trigeminal nerve (mandibular branch, via nerve to tensor tympani) and facial nerve (for stapedius)

special-senses/ear-anatomy-and-vestibula.sc: A cross-sectional diagram of the cochlea shows three fluid-filled compartments (scala vestibuli, scala media, scala tympani) separated by two membranes, with the organ of Corti resting on one of them.
tk: Name the three scalae and the fluid contained within each.
Name the two membranes separating the scalae.
Identify the membrane on which the organ of Corti rests.
State the tonotopic organization of the basilar membrane (which region detects high versus low frequencies).
ck: Names scala vestibuli (perilymph), scala media (endolymph), scala tympani (perilymph)
Names Reissner's (vestibular) membrane and the basilar membrane
Identifies the basilar membrane
States the base of the cochlea (near the oval window) detects high frequencies, while the apex detects low frequencies

special-senses/ear-anatomy-and-vestibula.sc: A three-dimensional diagram shows the three semicircular canals oriented roughly perpendicular to one another, each with an ampulla containing sensory epithelium.
tk: Name the three semicircular canals and the plane each detects.
Name the sensory structure within the ampulla that detects rotational movement.
Explain the physiological mechanism by which endolymph movement is translated into a neural signal.
Name the vestibular structures (other than the semicircular canals) that detect linear acceleration and head position relative to gravity.
ck: Names lateral (horizontal), anterior (superior), and posterior semicircular canals, each detecting rotation roughly in its own plane
Names the crista ampullaris (with the cupula)
Explains endolymph movement deflects the cupula, bending stereocilia of hair cells and altering their firing rate
Names the utricle and saccule (maculae, containing otoliths)

special-senses/ear-anatomy-and-vestibula.t: Weber and Rinne Test Interpretation Station
special-senses/ear-anatomy-and-vestibula.sc: A clinical vignette describes a patient undergoing tuning fork testing: the Weber test lateralizes to the left ear, and the Rinne test on the left ear shows bone conduction greater than air conduction.
tk: Interpret the type of hearing loss suggested by these findings and identify the affected ear.
Explain the physiological principle underlying a normal (positive) Rinne test result.
State the expected Rinne test result pattern in sensorineural hearing loss.
Name one possible cause of the type of hearing loss demonstrated in this patient.
ck: Identifies conductive hearing loss in the left ear (Weber lateralizes to the affected/worse conductive ear, Rinne is negative/abnormal there)
Explains normally air conduction exceeds bone conduction since the ossicular chain provides amplification
States in sensorineural hearing loss, air conduction still exceeds bone conduction (Rinne remains positive) but both are reduced, and Weber lateralizes to the better/normal ear
Names a valid cause of conductive hearing loss (e.g., otosclerosis, otitis media with effusion, cerumen impaction)

special-senses/physiology-of-vision.sc: A diagram of a rod photoreceptor outer segment shows rhodopsin, transducin, and cGMP-gated channels, illustrating the response to a light stimulus.
tk: Name the visual pigment shown and its chromophore component.
Describe the sequence of events from light absorption to hyperpolarization of the photoreceptor.
State whether photoreceptors are depolarized or hyperpolarized in the dark, and explain why.
Name the neurotransmitter released by photoreceptors and the direction of change in its release with light exposure.
ck: Names rhodopsin, composed of opsin and retinal (11-cis-retinal)
Describes light isomerizing retinal, activating transducin, activating phosphodiesterase, which breaks down cGMP, closing cGMP-gated cation channels, causing hyperpolarization
States photoreceptors are relatively depolarized in the dark due to a steady 'dark current' through open cGMP-gated channels
Names glutamate, with decreased release in response to light (due to hyperpolarization)

special-senses/physiology-of-vision.sc: A table comparing rods and cones is partially completed, with columns for light sensitivity, color vision, visual acuity, and retinal distribution left blank for two features.
tk: Complete the comparison for light sensitivity and color vision capability of rods versus cones.
State the retinal distribution pattern of rods versus cones.
Explain why cones provide higher visual acuity than rods.
Name the retinal region containing exclusively cones, responsible for the sharpest central vision.
ck: States rods are highly sensitive (function in dim light/scotopic vision) but do not support color vision; cones require brighter light (photopic vision) and mediate color vision
States rods predominate in the peripheral retina, cones are concentrated centrally (especially the fovea)
Explains cones typically have less convergence onto retinal ganglion cells, preserving spatial resolution, whereas rods show greater convergence, increasing sensitivity but reducing acuity
Names the fovea centralis

special-senses/physiology-of-vision.sc: A diagram shows the lens changing shape as an object of regard moves from far to near, along with associated changes in ciliary muscle tone and pupil size.
tk: Describe the three components of the near (accommodation) reflex triad.
Explain the mechanism by which ciliary muscle contraction changes lens shape.
Name the cranial nerve mediating the efferent parasympathetic limb of this reflex.
State the age-related condition in which the lens loses elasticity, impairing accommodation.
ck: Names accommodation (lens thickening), pupillary constriction (miosis), and convergence of the eyes
Explains ciliary muscle contraction relaxes tension on the zonular fibers/suspensory ligaments, allowing the elastic lens to become more spherical/convex
Names the oculomotor nerve (CN III), via the Edinger-Westphal nucleus and ciliary ganglion
Names presbyopia

special-senses/physiology-of-vision.sc: An Ishihara pseudoisochromatic test plate is displayed, along with a history that the patient cannot distinguish the embedded number pattern that most individuals with normal color vision can identify.
tk: Name the photoreceptor type responsible for color vision and the three subtypes based on peak spectral sensitivity.
Name the most common type of inherited color vision deficiency and its typical inheritance pattern.
Explain why color vision deficiency of this type is much more common in males than females.
State one occupational implication of significant red-green color vision deficiency.
ck: Names cone photoreceptors, with short (blue), medium (green), and long (red) wavelength-sensitive subtypes
Names red-green color blindness, typically X-linked recessive
Explains males are hemizygous for the X chromosome, so a single defective allele causes the condition, while females require two defective alleles (being generally carriers if heterozygous)
States a valid implication (e.g., restrictions in certain piloting, electrical wiring, or transportation-related occupations)

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.sc: A photomicrograph of the retina shows several distinct cellular layers from the outer pigmented layer to the innermost ganglion cell layer.
tk: List the retinal layers in order from outermost (choroid side) to innermost (vitreous side).
Identify the layer containing rod and cone outer segments.
State the functional significance of the retinal pigment epithelium.
Explain why light must pass through several retinal layers before reaching the photoreceptors.
ck: Lists a reasonable order: retinal pigment epithelium, photoreceptor layer, outer nuclear layer, outer plexiform layer, inner nuclear layer, inner plexiform layer, ganglion cell layer, nerve fiber layer
Identifies the photoreceptor (rod and cone outer segment) layer
States the retinal pigment epithelium absorbs stray light, recycles retinoids, and supports photoreceptor metabolism
Explains the retina is an 'inverted' structure, with photoreceptors facing away from incoming light, situated behind the other neural layers

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.sc: A photomicrograph of the cochlear duct shows the organ of Corti resting on the basilar membrane, with inner and outer hair cells and the tectorial membrane visible above.
tk: Identify the inner and outer hair cells and state their primary functional roles.
Name the membrane overlying the stereocilia of the hair cells.
Explain the mechanism by which sound-induced basilar membrane vibration leads to hair cell stimulation.
State which hair cell type is primarily responsible for cochlear amplification (electromotility).
ck: States inner hair cells are the primary sensory receptors transmitting auditory information, while outer hair cells modulate/amplify the response
Names the tectorial membrane
Explains basilar membrane movement causes shearing between the tectorial membrane and stereocilia, bending them and opening mechanically gated ion channels
Names outer hair cells (via electromotility/prestin-mediated length changes)

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.t: Optic Vesicle and Cup Development Diagram
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.sc: A sequential diagram shows the optic vesicle evaginating from the forebrain, then invaginating to form the optic cup, with the lens placode developing adjacent to it.
tk: Name the embryonic structure from which the optic vesicle arises.
Name the two layers of the optic cup and their eventual adult derivatives.
Name the structure that induces lens placode formation from surface ectoderm.
Name the congenital defect resulting from failure of the choroid (optic) fissure to close.
ck: Names the diencephalon (forebrain neuroectoderm)
Names the outer layer forming retinal pigment epithelium and the inner layer forming the neural retina
Names the optic vesicle as inducing the overlying surface ectoderm to form the lens placode
Names coloboma

special-senses/special-senses-histology-.t: Taste Bud Histology and Distribution Station
special-senses/special-senses-histology-.sc: A photomicrograph of a circumvallate papilla on the tongue shows several flask-shaped taste buds embedded within the stratified squamous epithelium.
tk: Name the cell types found within a taste bud.
Name the cranial nerve carrying taste sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
Name the cranial nerve carrying taste sensation from the posterior one-third of the tongue.
State the five basic taste qualities detected by taste receptor cells.
ck: Names taste (gustatory) receptor cells, along with supporting and basal cells
Names the facial nerve (CN VII, via the chorda tympani)
Names the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
States sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and umami

special-senses/physiology-of-hearing-and.sc: A diagram shows a person's head rotating to the right while the eyes simultaneously move to the left to maintain fixation on a stationary target.
tk: Name the reflex demonstrated.
State the sensory structure providing the afferent signal for this reflex during head rotation.
Explain the functional purpose of this reflex during head movement.
Describe how this reflex can be assessed clinically at the bedside (e.g., doll's eye/oculocephalic testing).
ck: Names the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR)
Names the semicircular canals (specifically the horizontal canal for horizontal head rotation)
Explains the VOR stabilizes gaze on a target by producing eye movements equal and opposite to head movements, maintaining a stable retinal image
Describes the oculocephalic (doll's eye) maneuver, in which passive head turning produces conjugate eye deviation opposite to the direction of head movement if brainstem pathways are intact

special-senses/physiology-of-hearing-and.t: Traveling Wave Theory of Cochlear Frequency Analysis
special-senses/physiology-of-hearing-and.sc: A diagram shows the basilar membrane's traveling wave pattern in response to sounds of different frequencies, with the peak of displacement occurring at different locations along the membrane.
tk: Name the theory illustrated by this diagram.
Explain the mechanical basis for why the base of the basilar membrane responds maximally to high-frequency sound.
Explain the mechanical basis for why the apex responds maximally to low-frequency sound.
State the clinical relevance of this tonotopic arrangement to patterns of noise-induced hearing loss.
ck: Names the traveling wave theory (Bekesy's place theory)
Explains the base of the basilar membrane is narrow and stiff, resonating best with high frequencies
Explains the apex is wider and more compliant, resonating best with low frequencies
States noise-induced hearing loss classically first affects frequencies around 4000 Hz, corresponding to a specific basilar membrane region vulnerable to mechanical damage

special-senses/physiology-of-hearing-and.sc: A clinical vignette describes caloric testing, in which cold water is instilled into one ear canal, producing nystagmus with the slow phase toward the irrigated ear and fast phase away from it.
tk: Explain the physiological basis by which cold water instillation induces this response.
State the mnemonic used to remember the direction of nystagmus with cold versus warm water irrigation.
Explain why caloric testing is clinically useful in evaluating vestibular function or brainstem integrity in comatose patients.
State the expected finding if the tested labyrinth/vestibular nerve is non-functional.
ck: Explains cold water creates a convection current in the endolymph of the horizontal semicircular canal, mimicking a specific direction of rotation and altering vestibular nerve firing
States the COWS mnemonic (Cold Opposite, Warm Same, referring to fast-phase nystagmus direction)
Explains an intact response requires functioning peripheral vestibular apparatus and brainstem pathways, useful for assessing brainstem function in unconscious patients
States absent nystagmus response on the affected side, indicating a non-functional labyrinth or vestibular nerve

special-senses/physiology-of-hearing-and.t: Postural Balance and Sensory Integration Station
special-senses/physiology-of-hearing-and.sc: A diagram depicts three sensory inputs (visual, vestibular, and proprioceptive) converging on central pathways that generate postural adjustments to maintain balance.
tk: Name the three sensory systems contributing to postural balance shown in the diagram.
Explain what typically happens to balance when one of these inputs is removed (e.g., closing the eyes) in a healthy individual versus one with vestibular dysfunction.
Name the central structure most responsible for coordinating balance and motor output based on this sensory information.
State one clinical test used to assess the relative contribution of vestibular versus visual/proprioceptive input to balance.
ck: Names visual, vestibular, and proprioceptive (somatosensory) systems
Explains a healthy individual can compensate reasonably well using the remaining two systems, but a person with vestibular dysfunction becomes markedly more unsteady when visual input is removed
Names the cerebellum (with vestibular nuclei and brainstem integration)
Names the Romberg test

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.sc: A diagram of the neck shows the thyroid gland with its two lobes and isthmus, along with adjacent structures including the trachea, recurrent laryngeal nerves, and parathyroid glands.
tk: Name the structures at risk of injury during thyroidectomy, based on their close relationship to the thyroid gland.
State the clinical consequence of unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury.
State the clinical consequence of bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury.
Name the artery that must be identified and preserved to protect the parathyroid glands during thyroid surgery.
ck: Names the recurrent laryngeal nerves and parathyroid glands (and superior laryngeal nerve) as at-risk structures
States hoarseness of voice due to unilateral vocal cord paralysis
States potential airway obstruction from bilateral vocal cord paralysis, a surgical emergency
Names the inferior thyroid artery

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.t: Pituitary Gland and Optic Chiasm Relations Station
endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.sc: A sagittal diagram of the skull base shows the pituitary gland within the sella turcica, with the optic chiasm positioned directly superior to it.
tk: Explain why a pituitary macroadenoma often produces bitemporal visual field loss.
Name the venous structures on either side of the pituitary at risk during transsphenoidal surgery.
Name the surgical approach typically used to access the pituitary gland, based on this anatomical relationship.
Name the cranial nerves that pass through the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus, at risk with lateral pituitary tumor extension.
ck: Explains superior extension of a pituitary tumor can compress the overlying optic chiasm, affecting decussating nasal retinal fibers
Names the cavernous sinuses
Names the transsphenoidal approach
Names oculomotor (III), trochlear (IV), ophthalmic and maxillary divisions of trigeminal (V1, V2), and abducens (VI) nerves

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.sc: A photomicrograph of the adrenal gland shows three distinct cortical zones with differing cellular arrangements, overlying a darker-staining medullary region.
tk: Identify the three cortical zones from outer to inner and the principal hormone class secreted by each.
Identify the medullary cell type and its secretory products.
State the germ layer origin of the adrenal cortex versus the adrenal medulla.
Explain why the adrenal medulla is considered functionally analogous to a sympathetic ganglion.
ck: Names zona glomerulosa (mineralocorticoids), zona fasciculata (glucocorticoids), zona reticularis (androgens)
Names chromaffin cells secreting catecholamines (epinephrine and norepinephrine)
States the cortex arises from mesoderm, while the medulla arises from neural crest ectoderm
Explains chromaffin cells are modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons lacking axons, releasing hormones directly into the bloodstream rather than at a synapse

endocrine-and-reproductive/endocrine-gla.sc: A photomicrograph shows small, densely packed polygonal cells with round nuclei arranged in cords, admixed with a smaller number of larger, more eosinophilic cells, adjacent to adipose tissue.
tk: Identify the gland shown and the two cell types visible.
State the primary secretory product of the predominant cell type.
Explain how age-related increase in adipose tissue within this gland can affect its imaging appearance.
Name one embryological structure from which the parathyroid glands are derived.
ck: Identifies the parathyroid gland, showing chief (principal) cells and oxyphil cells
States chief cells secrete parathyroid hormone (PTH)
Explains increasing fat content with age can make the gland appear less dense/more difficult to distinguish radiologically
Names the third and fourth pharyngeal (branchial) pouches

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.sc: A flow diagram shows CRH from the hypothalamus stimulating ACTH from the anterior pituitary, which stimulates cortisol release from the adrenal cortex, with feedback arrows returning to the hypothalamus and pituitary.
tk: Name the hormones at each level of this axis (hypothalamus, pituitary, adrenal).
Explain the type of feedback shown by the arrows returning from cortisol to the hypothalamus and pituitary.
State the expected effect of chronic exogenous glucocorticoid therapy on this axis.
Explain why abrupt cessation of long-term steroid therapy can precipitate adrenal insufficiency.
ck: Names CRH, ACTH, and cortisol
States negative feedback, in which cortisol suppresses further CRH and ACTH secretion
States chronic exogenous glucocorticoids suppress endogenous CRH/ACTH secretion and cause adrenal cortical atrophy
Explains the suppressed/atrophied adrenal cortex cannot promptly resume adequate endogenous cortisol production if steroids are stopped abruptly, risking adrenal insufficiency

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.sc: A graph shows plasma insulin and glucagon concentrations plotted against time relative to a meal, with insulin rising sharply after eating and glucagon rising during a subsequent fasting period.
tk: Explain the physiological trigger for the postprandial rise in insulin shown.
State the combined effect of high insulin and low glucagon on hepatic glucose metabolism after a meal.
State the combined effect of low insulin and high glucagon during fasting.
Name the cell types secreting insulin and glucagon respectively.
ck: Explains rising blood glucose (and amino acids) after a meal stimulates beta cell insulin secretion
States promotion of glycogen synthesis and inhibition of glycogenolysis/gluconeogenesis (net glucose storage)
States promotion of glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, raising blood glucose to maintain fasting glucose levels
Names beta cells (insulin) and alpha cells (glucagon)

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.sc: A table compares the actions of parathyroid hormone, calcitonin, and vitamin D on bone, kidney, and intestine, with several cells left blank.
tk: Complete the effect of parathyroid hormone on bone and kidney calcium/phosphate handling.
Complete the effect of calcitonin on serum calcium and its cell of origin.
State the primary action of activated vitamin D (calcitriol) relevant to intestinal calcium absorption.
Explain how these three hormones work together to maintain calcium homeostasis in the face of a sudden hypocalcemic stimulus.
ck: States PTH increases bone resorption (raising serum calcium) and increases renal calcium reabsorption while decreasing renal phosphate reabsorption
States calcitonin (from parafollicular/C cells) lowers serum calcium by inhibiting osteoclastic bone resorption
States calcitriol increases intestinal calcium (and phosphate) absorption

Explains falling calcium stimulates PTH release, which mobilizes calcium from bone, retains renal calcium, and stimulates renal calcitriol synthesis to enhance intestinal absorption, correcting the hypocalcemia

endocrine-and-reproductive/hormone-physi.sc: A diagram shows hypothalamic GHRH stimulating pituitary growth hormone release, which acts on the liver to produce IGF-1, with negative feedback from both GH and IGF-1.
tk: Name the hypothalamic hormones that stimulate and inhibit growth hormone release, respectively.
Explain the primary mediator of GH's growth-promoting effects on bone and cartilage.
State the consequence of excess GH secretion occurring before epiphyseal plate closure.
State the consequence of excess GH secretion occurring after epiphyseal plate closure.
ck: Names growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH, stimulatory) and somatostatin (inhibitory)
States IGF-1 (produced mainly by the liver in response to GH) mediates most of the growth-promoting anabolic effects
States gigantism (excessive linear growth)
