States acromegaly (bone thickening and soft tissue overgrowth without increased height)

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.sc: A diagram shows the sequential stages of spermatogenesis within the seminiferous tubule, from spermatogonia through primary and secondary spermatocytes to spermatids and spermatozoa.
tk: List the sequential cell types in order from spermatogonium to mature spermatozoon.
State at which stage(s) meiotic division(s) occur.
State the approximate total duration of spermatogenesis in humans.
Name the cell layer/structure that creates distinct basal and adluminal compartments within the seminiferous tubule.
ck: Lists spermatogonium, primary spermatocyte, secondary spermatocyte, spermatid, spermatozoon (with spermiogenesis as the final step)
States meiosis I occurs at the primary spermatocyte stage (producing secondary spermatocytes) and meiosis II at the secondary spermatocyte stage (producing spermatids)
States approximately 64-74 days
Names Sertoli cell tight junctions forming the blood-testis barrier

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.t: Testicular Descent and Hernia Relations Diagram
endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.sc: A diagram traces the path of testicular descent from the posterior abdominal wall through the inguinal canal into the scrotum, with the processus vaginalis shown alongside the testis.
tk: Name the structure that guides testicular descent.
State the fate of the processus vaginalis in normal development.
Name the condition resulting from a patent processus vaginalis allowing peritoneal fluid to accumulate around the testis.
Name the condition resulting from a patent processus vaginalis wide enough to allow bowel to herniate into the scrotum.
ck: Names the gubernaculum
States it normally obliterates, becoming a fibrous remnant, leaving only the tunica vaginalis around the testis
Names congenital (communicating) hydrocele
Names indirect inguinal hernia (congenital type, extending into the scrotum)

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.sc: A semen analysis report is provided showing sperm concentration, motility percentage, and morphology percentage, compared against reference values.
tk: State the approximate lower reference limit for sperm concentration according to standard semen analysis criteria.
Define the term used for a sperm concentration below the reference range.
Explain why both sperm motility and morphology are assessed in addition to concentration when evaluating fertility potential.
Name one lifestyle or environmental factor known to adversely affect semen parameters.
ck: States approximately 15 million sperm per mL (or a similar standard reference figure)
Names oligozoospermia (or oligospermia)
Explains adequate numbers alone are insufficient for fertility if sperm cannot move effectively toward the oocyte or have abnormal morphology impairing function/fertilization
Names a valid factor (e.g., smoking, heat exposure, alcohol excess, certain medications)

endocrine-and-reproductive/male-reproduc.sc: A diagram shows the vas deferens ligated and divided bilaterally as part of a vasectomy procedure, at a point proximal to the seminal vesicles.
tk: Explain the immediate physiological consequence of vasectomy on fertility.
Explain why ejaculate volume is not markedly reduced after vasectomy, despite the absence of sperm.
State why a period of continued contraceptive use is recommended immediately after vasectomy before relying on it alone.
Explain the physiological fate of sperm continuously produced by the testis after vasectomy.
ck: Explains sperm can no longer travel from the epididymis into the ejaculate, preventing fertilization
Explains most ejaculate volume comes from the seminal vesicles and prostate, structures unaffected by vasectomy, distal to the ligation site
States residual sperm may remain in the distal vas deferens/ejaculatory ducts, requiring several ejaculations or a set time period (and often a semen check) to clear before sterility is confirmed
Explains sperm are reabsorbed (phagocytosed) within the epididymis and proximal vas deferens

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.sc: A composite graph shows plasma estrogen, progesterone, LH, and FSH levels plotted across a standard 28-day menstrual cycle, alongside corresponding endometrial and ovarian changes.
tk: Identify the approximate day of the LH surge and the ovulatory event it triggers.
Describe the change in the endometrium during the proliferative versus secretory phases.
Explain the hormonal basis for the sharp fall in estrogen and progesterone that precedes menstruation, assuming no pregnancy.
State the approximate duration of the luteal phase, and explain why it is relatively constant compared to the follicular phase.
ck: States the LH surge occurs around day 14, triggering ovulation approximately 36 hours later
Describes estrogen-driven endometrial proliferation (proliferative phase) followed by progesterone-driven secretory transformation (secretory phase)
Explains corpus luteum regression (in the absence of hCG/pregnancy) leads to falling progesterone and estrogen, withdrawing endometrial support and triggering shedding
States approximately 14 days, reflecting the fixed lifespan of the corpus luteum unless rescued by hCG

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.sc: A sequential diagram shows follicular development from primordial follicle through primary, secondary, and Graafian (mature) follicle stages, with a fluid-filled antrum appearing at one stage.
tk: Identify the stage at which the antrum first appears.
Name the layer of granulosa cells surrounding the oocyte that remains attached to it at ovulation.
Explain the concept of follicular dominance/selection occurring during the mid-follicular phase.
State the fate of follicles that do not achieve dominance during a given cycle.
ck: States the antrum appears at the secondary (antral) follicle stage
Names the corona radiata (cumulus oophorus complex)
Explains multiple follicles begin developing, but typically one becomes dominant (most FSH-sensitive/estrogen-producing), suppressing further FSH support for the remaining cohort
States non-dominant follicles undergo atresia

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.t: Breast Anatomy and Lactation Structure Diagram
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.sc: A diagram of the breast shows lobules, lactiferous ducts, and lactiferous sinuses converging toward the nipple, with surrounding adipose and connective tissue.
tk: Name the functional secretory unit of the breast responsible for milk production.
Name the structure where milk is stored just before reaching the nipple.
Name the cell type responsible for milk ejection via contraction, and the hormone that stimulates it.
Name the hormone primarily responsible for milk synthesis by glandular epithelial cells.
ck: Names the lobule (containing alveoli/acini) as the secretory unit
Names the lactiferous sinus (ampulla)
Names myoepithelial cells, stimulated by oxytocin
Names prolactin

endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.t: Cervical Mucus and Ovulation Prediction Station
endocrine-and-reproductive/female-reprod.sc: A series of cervical mucus samples collected across a menstrual cycle are displayed, showing progressive changes in consistency, clarity, and elasticity, with one sample stretching into a long thin thread between two glass slides.
tk: Identify the phase of the menstrual cycle corresponding to the highly elastic, thread-forming mucus sample.
Name the term used to describe the stretchability of cervical mucus and its clinical use in fertility assessment.
Explain the hormonal basis for the change from thick, scant mucus to thin, watery mucus around this phase.
State how cervical mucus changes again after ovulation and the hormone responsible.
ck: Identifies the periovulatory phase (around the time of the LH surge/ovulation)
Names spinnbarkeit, used as a fertility-awareness indicator of the fertile window
Explains rising estrogen from the maturing dominant follicle thins and increases the elasticity of cervical mucus, facilitating sperm transport
States mucus becomes thick and scant again under progesterone influence from the corpus luteum after ovulation

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.sc: A graph plots maternal serum hCG, progesterone, and estriol concentrations across the three trimesters of pregnancy.
tk: Describe the characteristic pattern of hCG levels across pregnancy (peak timing and subsequent trend).
Explain the physiological reason for the early hCG peak in relation to corpus luteum support.
State the trend of progesterone and estriol levels as pregnancy progresses toward term.
State the clinical utility of serial estriol or hCG measurement in assessing certain pregnancy complications.
ck: Describes hCG rising rapidly in the first trimester, peaking around 8-10 weeks, then declining and plateauing at a lower level for the remainder of pregnancy
Explains the early peak coincides with hCG's role in maintaining the corpus luteum before the luteal-placental shift, after which placental progesterone production takes over
States progesterone and estriol both rise progressively toward term as the placenta grows
States abnormal trends (e.g., low estriol) may be used as part of assessing fetoplacental well-being or specific fetal conditions

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.sc: A set of three diagrams shows different combinations of chorionicity and amnionicity in twin pregnancies: dichorionic-diamniotic, monochorionic-diamniotic, and monochorionic-monoamniotic.
tk: Explain how the timing of embryonic splitting determines chorionicity and amnionicity in monozygotic twins.
Identify which chorionicity pattern is always associated with dizygotic twins.
State the highest-risk chorionicity pattern for twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome and cord entanglement, respectively.
Explain why ultrasound determination of chorionicity is clinically important early in twin pregnancies.
ck: Explains splitting within the first few days produces dichorionic-diamniotic twins; splitting between days 4-8 produces monochorionic-diamniotic twins; splitting after day 8 produces monochorionic-monoamniotic twins (and after day 13, conjoined twins)
States dizygotic twins are always dichorionic-diamniotic
States monochorionic-diamniotic pregnancies carry the highest risk of twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome, while monochorionic-monoamniotic pregnancies carry the highest risk of cord entanglement
Explains chorionicity determines the level of risk and monitoring needs, so accurate early determination guides appropriate pregnancy surveillance

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.t: Ambiguous Genitalia / Disorder of Sex Development Diagram
endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.sc: A diagram illustrates the bipotential external genitalia and the divergent pathways of male and female differentiation, alongside a case description of a newborn with atypical genital appearance.
tk: Name the hormone(s) required for normal male external genital virilization.
Explain what pattern of genital development would be expected in a genetic male (46,XY) with complete androgen insensitivity.
Explain what pattern of genital development would be expected in a genetic female (46,XX) exposed to excess androgens in utero (e.g., congenital adrenal hyperplasia).
State why karyotyping and hormonal assessment are essential steps in evaluating a newborn with ambiguous genitalia.
ck: Names testosterone (for internal duct differentiation) and dihydrotestosterone (for external genitalia/prostate virilization)
Explains despite normal or high testosterone, receptor insensitivity prevents virilization, resulting in female-appearing external genitalia despite a 46,XY karyotype and testes
Explains excess androgen exposure can virilize female external genitalia (e.g., clitoromegaly, labial fusion) despite a normal 46,XX karyotype and ovaries
Explains karyotype and hormone levels help distinguish the underlying category of disorder of sex development, guiding appropriate management and counseling

endocrine-and-reproductive/reproductive-.sc: A flow diagram shows cholesterol being converted stepwise by the fetal adrenal gland, fetal liver, and placenta into estriol, illustrating cooperative steroidogenesis.
tk: Name the initial steroid precursor produced by the fetal adrenal gland in this pathway.
State the modification made by the fetal liver to this precursor before it reaches the placenta.
Explain why the placenta alone cannot synthesize estriol without fetal contribution.
State why maternal serum/urinary estriol was historically used as a marker of fetal well-being.
ck: Names dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEA-S)
States 16-alpha-hydroxylation of DHEA-S in the fetal liver

Explains the placenta lacks certain enzymes (such as 17-alpha-hydroxylase/19-hydroxylase pathway components) needed to produce the androgen precursors itself, relying on fetal adrenal and liver contributions before aromatization
Explains estriol levels reflect both fetal adrenal/liver function and placental function, so a falling level could suggest fetoplacental compromise
